newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: NATO hopefuls lobby hard at ministerial meet.
newsitem.headline: NATO hopefuls lobby hard at ministerial meet.

text.p: Possible new NATO members lobbied hard at a ministerial meeting of the military alliance on Friday, with outside bets such as Romania and Slovenia sensing the odds on membership may be shortening.

Until now, only three former communist states, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Poland had been seen as near certainties to win access to the 16-nation group when a final decision on enlargement is taken in Madrid next month.

But with NATO foreign ministers clearly split on the issue of just how many of the former Soviet bloc states should be admitted in the first wave, Slovenia and Romania were seizing the chance for a hard sell of their countries' candidacies.
"Membership of Romania is important not only for Romania but for NATO. Romania could strengthen the vulnerable flank (of the organisation)," Foreign Minister Adrian Severin told journalists.

Ministers from 27 European countries which are not members of NATO had gathered together with the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) states at this picturesque Portuguese mountain resort for the launch of a new body aimed at meeting some of their security concerns.

The Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council (EAPC), which will have a permanent secretariat at NATO's Brussels headquarters, merges the alliance's military cooperation programme and a forum for political dialogue with non-member countries.
NATO ministers were cagey following an initial round of discussions on Thursday on just how many new members should be admitted in July.

But diplomats said that there was a clear split between the United States and some European allies which favoured just three new members, and other European countries who backed a more ambitious approach.

"There are no final decisions (yet) on membership (but) there is a consensus on three countries and growing support for two more," said Hungarian Foreign Minister Laszio Kovacs told journalists after the EAPC meeting.
NATO's southern flank countries such as Italy, Spain and Portugal are known to favour a wider membership, but diplomatic sources said that Canada and Britain were also prepared to go beyond three.

"It is clear that the Europeans are relatively more ambitious after the deal with Russia," said Slovenian Foreign Minister Zoran Thaler, referring to the historic cooperation charter signed earlier this week between Moscow and NATO.
The accord with Russia cleared the way for NATO to expand eastwards, absorbing some former members of the Soviet bloc.
"There is now space for a balanced enlargement involving both the northern and southern NATO areas," Thaler said.
Despite the debate over the exact number of countries to admit in a first wave, NATO ministers have been adamant that the door remains open for further arrivals in the future.
But Thaler said that he had noted fears that opening the door too wide first time round could delay a future second wave.

Ministers from the Baltic states said that they were reassured by NATO's firm stand against Russian attempts to impose a veto on Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania eventually becoming members of the alliance.
Estonia's Foreign Minister Toomas Hendrik Ilves told a news conference that it would be symbolic if the next round of enlargement could begin in April 1999, NATO's 50th birthday.
